name: Robinson-Trautman Radiating Spacetimes
description: The vacuum field of an isolated body sending out gravitational waves on expanding wave fronts, found by Ivor Robinson and Andrzej Trautman in 1960. From smooth initial data the fronts grow round as the waves leave, and the spacetime settles down to the Schwarzschild black hole.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ and $G$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$. The mass parameter is $m = GM/c^2$, a length.
history: Ivor Robinson and Andrzej Trautman found in 1960 the vacuum spacetimes that contain a family of light rays spreading apart without shear and without twist [robinson1960, griffiths2009]. Rays without twist are orthogonal to a family of null hypersurfaces, the wave fronts of constant retarded time $u$, and the affine parameter $r$ along each ray is the radial coordinate [robinson1962, podolsky2009]. Robinson and Trautman reduced Einstein's equations for every such spacetime to one equation of fourth order for a function $P$ on the surfaces of constant $u$ and $r$ [robinson1960, griffiths2009]. They published the derivation in 1962 and showed the solutions to be algebraically special, of Petrov type II, III, N, or D [robinson1962, stephani2003]. The solutions of type D include Schwarzschild's and the C-metric [robinson1962, griffiths2009].¶With $P = P_0 = 1 + \zeta\bar\zeta/2$, where $\zeta$ is a complex stereographic coordinate, the wave fronts are round spheres and the metric is Schwarzschild's in retarded time [bicak1997]. For any other $P$ the Gaussian curvature $K = \Delta\ln P$ of the fronts, with $\Delta$ the Laplacian on the wave front, varies over the sphere, and the Robinson-Trautman equation, $\partial_u\ln P = -\Delta K/(12m)$, evolves $P$ in $u$ [podolsky2009]. In the null tetrad of the rays the Weyl tensor has $\Psi_2 = -m/r^3$, and its components $\Psi_3$ and $\Psi_4$ are built from derivatives of $K$ and of $\partial_u\ln P$, with $\Psi_4$ falling off as $1/r$ [podolsky2009]. David Singleton wrote the Bondi mass in 1990 as $M_B = (m/4\pi)\oint (P_0/P)^3\,d\Omega$ [chow1999]. It decreases as $u$ advances and stays above $m$ when the fronts are scaled to the area $4\pi r^2$ [chow1999]. No radiation comes in from infinity in these spacetimes [chow1999].¶J. Foster and Ezra Newman perturbed the Schwarzschild solution in 1967 and obtained approximate solutions, consistent with the Bondi-Sachs radiation conditions for bounded sources, that are Schwarzschild in the asymptotic future [foster1967]. Béla Lukács, Zoltán Perjés, J. Porter, and Ákos Sebestyén showed in 1984 that the integral of $K^2$ over a wave front decreases along every solution, so that a solution existing for all $u$ converges to Schwarzschild's [lukacs1984, chow1999]. Bernd Schmidt proved in 1988 that solutions exist locally for sufficiently differentiable initial data [schmidt1988, chow1999]. Alan Rendall proved the same year that they exist for all later $u$ when the initial data are small and symmetric under the antipodal map of the sphere, and Singleton removed the symmetry in 1990 [rendall1988, singleton1990, chow1999].¶Piotr Chruściel proved in 1991 that for smooth initial data of any size the solution exists for all later retarded times and converges to a metric of constant curvature on the sphere, Schwarzschild's [chrusciel1991, bicak1997]. The equation is the Calabi equation in two dimensions, named for the flow of Kähler metrics Eugenio Calabi introduced in 1982 [calabi1982, chrusciel1991]. Toward the past a general solution diverges, so the spacetime has no past null infinity [chow1999, podolsky2009]. The approach to Schwarzschild is exponential, $P/P_0 = 1 + f_{1,0}\,e^{-2u/m} + \dots$, and at the fifteenth order a term $u\,e^{-30u/m}$ appears [chrusciel1992, bicak1997]. The surface $u = \infty$ is the event horizon of the Schwarzschild black hole, and Chruściel showed in 1992 that every such spacetime can be extended across it as a metric of class $C^{117}$ [chrusciel1992]. He and Singleton proved the same year that the coefficient of $u\,e^{-30u/m}$ is nonzero for some spacetimes, which therefore have no smooth extension [chruscielsingleton1992, bicak1997].¶The curvature singularity at $r = 0$ is spacelike and lies in the past, a white hole [chow1999]. Roger Penrose's 1973 equation $K - 2m/\mathcal{R} = \Delta\ln\mathcal{R}$ locates on each wave front a surface $r = \mathcal{R}$ whose ingoing light rays neither converge nor diverge [penrose1973, chow1999]. Paul Tod proved in 1989 that the equation has a unique smooth solution and that the surface is the outer boundary of the past trapped surfaces on its front [tod1989, chow1999]. Ernest Chow and Anthony Lun showed in 1999 that these surfaces sweep out a hypersurface that is nowhere timelike, the past apparent horizon, whose area $A$ decreases as $u$ advances [chow1999]. The area obeys $16\pi m^2 \le A \le 16\pi M_B^2$, the lower bound Chow and Lun's and the upper Tod's [chow1999].¶Jiří Bičák and Jiří Podolský added a cosmological constant in 1995: for $\Lambda > 0$ and $9\Lambda m^2 < 1$ the spacetimes settle down to Schwarzschild-de Sitter, and every geodesic observer sees the metric inside the past light cone approach de Sitter's [bicak1995, bicak1997]. In 1997 they showed that the extension across the horizon is smoother for $\Lambda > 0$ than for $\Lambda = 0$, less smooth for $\Lambda < 0$, and at $9\Lambda m^2 = 1$ smooth and not analytic [bicak1997]. Podolský and Otakar Svítek carried Penrose's and Tod's equation over to $\Lambda \neq 0$ in 2009 and proved that the past horizon exists, is unique, and is spacelike [podolsky2009]. Rodrigo Macedo and Alberto Saa showed in 2008 that axisymmetric initial data without reflection symmetry evolve into a Schwarzschild black hole moving at constant speed, the recoil from the momentum its gravitational waves carry off [macedo2008]. Luciano Rezzolla, Macedo, and José Luis Jaramillo used these spacetimes in 2010 to study the "antikick", the sudden deceleration after the merger of two black holes, and found that the anisotropic distribution of curvature on the horizon of the deformed hole correlates with the direction and intensity of the recoil [rezzolla2010].

related.text: The quiet member, with round wave fronts and no radiation. Piotr Chruściel proved in 1991 that the others settle down to it as their waves leave [chrusciel1991, bicak1997].
Waves whose fronts are planes and whose rays stay parallel, where Robinson and Trautman's fronts expand [brinkmann1925, griffiths2009].
Two black holes accelerating apart, a member of the family of type D [robinson1962, griffiths2009].

A member with pure radiation in place of the vacuum, whose fronts stay round while the body accelerates on the recoil of its light. Its news function vanishes, so it sends out no gravitational waves [dain1996, cornish2000].

The member with round wave fronts and pure radiation in place of the vacuum, a star that shines evenly. Jiří Podolský and Otakar Svítek showed in 2005 that the other members with pure radiation approach it [podolsky2005].
Waves of the same algebraic type with a negative cosmological constant, on fronts that do not expand: hyperbolic planes crossing anti-de Sitter space [podolsky1998, bicak1999].
The waves of the same type whose rays do not expand. A wave of type N without twist belongs to one class or the other, with or without a cosmological constant [bicak1999].

parameters.description: Dimensionless function fixing the metric $r^2P^{-2}(dx^2 + dy^2)$ of each wave front, whose Gaussian curvature at $r = 1$ is $K = P^2(\partial_x^2 + \partial_y^2)\ln P$; $P = 1 + (x^2 + y^2)/4$ makes the fronts round spheres, and in vacuum $P$ obeys the Robinson-Trautman equation $P^2(\partial_x^2 + \partial_y^2)K + 12m\,\partial_u\ln P = 0$, which no component assumes
Dimensionless function, $2H = K - 2r\,\partial_u\ln P - 2m/r$ in vacuum, which no component assumes

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(u, r, x, y)$, with the retarded time $u$ carrying dimensions of time, $r$ an affine length along the rays, and $x$ and $y$ pure numbers on each wave front, where $\zeta = (x + iy)/\sqrt{2}$ is the complex stereographic coordinate. We take components in the chart $x^0 = cu$, so $\partial_u P = c^{-1}\partial P/\partial u$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{u}$ means $d(cu)/d\lambda$.
